title: Linkability of sensor telemetry across time and contexts
description: Continuous capture of GPS position, timestamps, heart rate, and step counts enables linking of data points to reconstruct user movement patterns, daily routines, and location history, potentially revealing sensitive behavioral information.
assumptions: Adversary has access to multiple data points or can correlate with external data sources

title: Identifiability through biometric and location data
description: Heart rate patterns, step counts, and GPS position data can be used to uniquely identify the wearer, especially when combined with timestamps and location information that may reveal home/work locations.
assumptions: Adversary has access to sufficient data points to perform identification

title: Unauthorized disclosure of sensor telemetry
description: Sensor data (heart rate, GPS, step counts) may be transmitted to unauthorized third parties, cloud services, or applications without proper consent or security controls.
assumptions: Data transmission channels lack adequate encryption or access controls

title: Tampering with sensor telemetry data
description: Sensor data could be modified, altered, or falsified by an adversary with access to the device, compromising the integrity of health and location information.
assumptions: Adversary has physical or logical access to the wearable device

title: Linkability of health data across systems
description: Calorie, meal, and weight data entered by the user could be linked with other health data sources (e.g., wearable devices, medical records) to create a comprehensive health profile of the user.
assumptions: The app may share data with third-party services or other systems that have access to the user's health information.
uncertainty_note: Using generic threat tree node L.1.1 as specific context not fully covered in retrieved knowledge

title: Identifiability of user from health data
description: The combination of weight entries, meal logs, and user profile information could potentially identify the specific user, especially if the data is shared or analyzed in aggregate.
assumptions: Health data combined with other identifiers could uniquely identify the user.
uncertainty_note: Using generic threat tree node I.1.1 as specific context not fully covered in retrieved knowledge

title: Unauthorized disclosure of personal health data
description: The companion app could potentially disclose the user's calorie, meal, and weight data to unauthorized third parties, either through security vulnerabilities, improper data sharing practices, or inadequate access controls.
assumptions: The app may transmit data to cloud services, third-party APIs, or other systems without proper authorization.
uncertainty_note: Using generic threat tree node D.1.1 as specific context not fully covered in retrieved knowledge

title: Explicit Health Data Disclosure to Data Store
description: The Companion Mobile App (P2) explicitly transfers personal health data (calorie intake, weight history, exercise sessions) to the Health Log Store (DS1). This constitutes a data disclosure across a system boundary, where health information is transferred from the app to a data store. The minimality principle should be evaluated to ensure only necessary health data is stored.
assumptions: The data store may be accessible by third parties or the organization operating it, creating potential for further disclosure.
uncertainty_note: Tree node Dd.1.1 is a reasonable choice for explicit disclosure; context [5] supports Dd as applicable for Process→DataStore flows.

title: Health Data Identifiability Risk
description: Health logs containing calorie intake, weight history, and exercise sessions may be personally identifiable when combined with other data sources. Weight patterns, exercise routines, and dietary habits can create unique behavioral profiles that could identify individuals even without explicit identifiers.
assumptions: Health data is considered sensitive personal data under regulations like GDPR and HIPAA, making identifiability a significant concern.
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is a standard identifiability node; context [3] confirms I is applicable at S/fl/D positions for Process→DataStore flows.

title: Health Log Data Integrity Risk
description: Health logs stored in DS1 could be altered, corrupted, or tampered with by unauthorized actors. This could affect medical decisions, insurance claims, or health tracking accuracy. Data integrity is critical for health-related data.
assumptions: The data store may not have adequate access controls or integrity verification mechanisms.
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 is a standard data integrity node; context [3] confirms D is applicable at S/fl/D positions for Process→DataStore flows.

title: Health Data Linkability Risk
description: Health log data could be linked to other data sources (e.g., user profiles, location data, purchase history) to create comprehensive user profiles. This linkability could enable tracking of individuals across different contexts and services.
assumptions: The health log store may be integrated with other systems or accessible to third parties who could correlate data.
uncertainty_note: Tree node L.1.1 is a standard linkability node; context [3] confirms L is applicable at S/fl/D positions for Process→DataStore flows.

title: Unintended Location Data Disclosure to Third Parties
description: GPS location traces with timestamps written to the location history store may be disclosed to third parties beyond intended recipients, violating the minimality principle. Location data is highly sensitive personal information that could reveal user movements, routines, and sensitive locations (e.g., home, workplace, healthcare facilities).
assumptions: The location history store may have access controls that are insufficient, or the data may be shared with partners, advertisers, or other entities without explicit user consent.
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 as a reasonable tree node for data disclosure threats in Process→DataStore flows based on context [5].

title: Location Data Enables User Identification and Tracking
description: GPS location traces with timestamps can be used to identify and track specific individuals. Even without direct identifiers, the combination of location patterns, timestamps, and device metadata can uniquely identify users and reveal their daily routines, social connections, and sensitive activities.
assumptions: Location data can be correlated with other data sources (e.g., social media, device IDs) to identify individuals. The granularity of GPS data (e.g., 10-50 meter accuracy) is sufficient for precise tracking.
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.1 as a reasonable tree node for identifiability threats in Process→DataStore flows.

title: Location Data Stored Without Adequate Access Controls
description: The location history store may lack proper access controls, allowing unauthorized access to stored location data. This creates a risk of data disclosure through breaches, insider threats, or improper access by system administrators.
assumptions: The data store may not implement encryption at rest, proper authentication, or audit logging. Location data stored in DS2 could be accessed by unauthorized parties.
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.2 as a reasonable tree node for data disclosure threats originating from DataStore elements.

title: Unintended Health Data Disclosure During Analytics Processing
description: Health log data (calorie, weight, exercise logs) is transferred from the Health Log Store to the Analytics Service for health-condition analysis. This represents an explicit data disclosure across the DataStore-Process boundary. The disclosure may be avoidable if the analytics service could operate with aggregated or anonymized data instead of individual-level logs.
assumptions: The analytics service requires individual-level health data to perform health-condition analysis, but this may not be strictly necessary if aggregation or anonymization techniques could be applied.
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 based on context [5] which describes data disclosure as transfer across boundaries. The exact tree_node may vary in LINDDUN Pro.

title: Linkability of Health Log Data Across Sessions
description: The analytics service reads calorie, weight, and exercise logs across multiple sessions, creating a longitudinal health profile that could be linked to identify specific individuals. This linkability threat arises from the aggregation of data points over time.
assumptions: Health logs contain sufficient detail to create identifiable health profiles when combined across sessions.
uncertainty_note: Tree node L.1.1 is inferred based on standard LINDDUN Pro structure for linkability threats.

title: Identifiability of Health Data Through Analytics Processing
description: The health-condition analysis performed by the analytics service processes personal health data that could directly or indirectly identify individuals. Weight, calorie, and exercise patterns are sensitive health indicators that may be traceable to specific users.
assumptions: Health data patterns are unique enough to identify individuals when analyzed.
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is inferred based on standard LINDDUN Pro structure for identifiability threats.

title: Profiling via Health Analytics Insights
description: Health analytics service may aggregate and analyze individual health data to produce insights that could reveal patterns about groups of individuals, potentially enabling profiling beyond the intended scope.
assumptions: Analytics service has access to sufficient historical data to identify group-level patterns; insights may be correlated across multiple data sources.
uncertainty_note: Citation L.2.2.2 from context is approximate - need to verify if this specific analytics flow actually performs group-level profiling.

title: Identity Inference from Health Risk Indicators
description: Inferred health-condition risk indicators and trend flags may contain sufficient detail to identify or re-identify the data subject, especially when combined with other known information.
assumptions: Health insights are specific enough to be linked to individuals; mobile app may have access to additional identifying information.
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is inferred from general LINDDUN methodology - exact node may vary by implementation.

title: Insufficient Cybersecurity Risk Management for Health Data
description: Health analytics data flow may lack proper cybersecurity risk management controls, creating gaps between privacy threats and broader risk management requirements, potentially violating regulatory obligations for health data protection.
assumptions: Health data is subject to regulatory requirements (e.g., HIPAA, GDPR); current risk management may not adequately address privacy-cybersecurity interplay.
uncertainty_note: Nc.3 citation from context is approximate - actual compliance requirements depend on jurisdiction and specific regulatory framework.

title: Excessive Health Indicator Display
description: The app dashboard displays inferred condition indicators (eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals) to the user, potentially revealing more sensitive health information than necessary for the intended functionality.
assumptions: The app may be displaying health risk signals that are more detailed than required for basic app operation.
uncertainty_note: Using D.1.1 based on general data minimization principles; exact tree node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: User Unawareness of Health Data Inference
description: Users may not be fully aware of how their health data is being processed to infer eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals, or what specific data sources are being used for these inferences.
assumptions: Privacy policies may not clearly explain the inference mechanisms or data sources used for health condition indicators.
uncertainty_note: U.1.1 is a general unawareness node; specific context about user consent and transparency mechanisms would strengthen this assessment.

title: Health Data Compliance Risk
description: Displaying sensitive health condition indicators (eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals) to users may create compliance risks under health data regulations (e.g., HIPAA, GDPR health data provisions) if proper consent, data minimization, and security measures are not implemented.
assumptions: Health data handling is subject to strict regulatory requirements that may not be fully addressed in the app's current implementation.
uncertainty_note: Nc.1.1 is a general non-compliance node; specific regulatory requirements for the app's jurisdiction would need verification.

title: Explicit Data Disclosure to Third-Party Cloud Provider
description: Full health and location dataset is explicitly transferred to external cloud hosting provider (EE2), representing intentional cross-boundary disclosure of personal data. This violates the minimality principle as the complete dataset is shared rather than only necessary subsets.
assumptions: The cloud provider has access to all health and location data without additional privacy controls

title: Identifiability of Health and Location Data
description: Health analytics data and location datasets contain personally identifiable information that can directly identify individuals. When hosted at third-party cloud provider, this identifiability persists and may be exploited.
assumptions: Health and location data are inherently identifiable without additional context

title: Linkability Across Systems and Time
description: Health and location data transferred to cloud provider can be linked with other datasets (e.g., other cloud services, external health records) to create comprehensive profiles of individuals, enabling cross-system correlation.
assumptions: Cloud provider may have access to or share data with other systems
uncertainty_note: Depends on cloud provider's data sharing practices and isolation measures
